title: B1 Writing Quiz 3 — Travel, Technology & Daily Life

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had more time, I would travel around the world.
If I have more time, I would travel around the world.
If I had more time, I will travel around the world.
If I would have more time, I would travel around the world.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I had more time, I would travel around the world.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If we had booked earlier, we wouldn't pay so much.
If we had booked earlier, we wouldn't have paid so much.
If we booked earlier, we wouldn't have paid so much.
If we would have booked earlier, we wouldn't have paid so much.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If we had booked..., we wouldn't have paid...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This app is used by millions of travelers.
This app uses by millions of travelers.
This app is using by millions of travelers.
This app use by millions of travelers.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is used by millions of travelers.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The bridge was built two hundred years ago.
The bridge built two hundred years ago.
The bridge was build two hundred years ago.
The bridge is built two hundred years ago.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was built two hundred years ago.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The engineer who designed the app used to be a teacher.
The engineer which designed the app used to be a teacher.
The engineer whom designed the app used to be a teacher.
The engineer, who designed the app, used to be a teacher but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The engineer who designed the app...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My new phone, which cost a fortune, broke after a week.
My new phone which cost a fortune broke after a week but.
My new phone, that cost a fortune, broke after a week.
My new phone which cost a fortune, broke after a week.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'My new phone, which cost a fortune, broke after a week.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He must be exhausted after such a long flight.
He must to be exhausted after such a long flight.
He must being exhausted after such a long flight.
He musts be exhausted after such a long flight.
questions.explanation: 'Must' + base verb expresses a confident positive deduction: 'he must be exhausted.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The flight might be delayed because of the storm.
The flight might being delayed because of the storm.
The flight might to be delayed because of the storm.
The flight mights be delayed because of the storm.
questions.explanation: 'Might' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the flight might be delayed.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've visited three countries this year.
I've been visiting three countries this year.
I've visit three countries this year.
I'm visiting three countries this year already.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've visited three countries.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been learning Spanish for two years.
I've learned Spanish since two years.
I'm learning Spanish for two years already.
I've been learn Spanish for two years.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been learning... for two years.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have booked the tickets.")
options: She said that she has booked the tickets.
She said that she had booked the tickets.
She said that she booked the tickets already.
She said she have booked the tickets.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'she had booked the tickets.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "Where are you staying?")
options: He asked me where do I stay.
He asked me where I was staying.
He asked me where did I stay.
He asked me where I stay.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'he asked me where I was staying.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to walk to school before we moved to the city.
I use to walk to school before we moved to the city.
I was used to walk to school before we moved to the city.
I used to walking to school before we moved to the city.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to walk to school.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm used to working from home now.
I'm used to work from home now.
I use to working from home now.
I'm used working to from home now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to working from home.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We had to put off the trip because of the weather.
We had to put the trip off because of the weather away.
We had to put off to the trip because of the weather.
We had to put the trip because of the weather off.
questions.explanation: 'Put off' means 'postpone': 'put off the trip.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We decided to set off early to avoid the traffic.
We decided to set the traffic off early.
We decided to set off to early the traffic.
We decided to set early off the traffic.
questions.explanation: 'Set off' means 'start a journey': 'set off early.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite the heavy rain, the match continued.
Despite of the heavy rain, the match continued.
Although the heavy rain, the match continued.
Despite the rain was heavy, the match continued.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the heavy rain, the match continued.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The flight was cancelled. As a result, we missed the connection.
The flight was cancelled, as a result we missed the connection.
As a result the flight was cancelled we missed the connection.
The flight was cancelled as a result, we missed the connection.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'The flight was cancelled. As a result, we missed the connection.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We didn't have enough time to see the whole museum.
We didn't have time enough to see the whole museum.
We didn't have enough of time to see the whole museum.
We hasn't enough time to see the whole museum.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough time.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She is in charge of the entire marketing department.
She is in charge for the entire marketing department.
She is charge of the entire marketing department.
She is on charge of the entire marketing department.
questions.explanation: 'In charge of' + noun means 'responsible for': 'in charge of the department.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a hotel manager you haven't met, asking about a booking?
options: Hey there,
Dear Sir or Madam,
Yo,
Hiya,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir or Madam,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a named contact you've corresponded with before?
options: Yours faithfully,
Best regards,
Later,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Best regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could recommend a good hotel nearby.
I was wondering if you could to recommend a good hotel nearby.
I was wondering could you recommending a good hotel nearby.
I wonder if you recommend could a good hotel nearby.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could recommend a hotel.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the guide.' and 'The guide's tours are famous.'?
options: This is the guide whose tours are famous.
This is the guide who tours are famous.
This is the guide which tours are famous.
This is the guide's tours who are famous.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the guide whose tours are famous.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never eaten such delicious food before.
I have eaten never such delicious food before.
Never I have eaten such delicious food before.
I have eaten such delicious food never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never eaten such food.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the train has already left.
I'd like to know whether has the train already left?
I'd like to know, whether the train has already left.
I'd like to know whether the train has already left?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time next week, I ___ on a beach in Spain.
options: will lie
will be lying
am lying
lie
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be lying'.

questions.question: By next summer, I ___ every country in Europe.
options: will visit
will have visited
visit
am visiting
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have visited'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly, pack your bags. Secondly, check your passport. Finally, book a taxi.
Firstly we pack bags secondly check finally taxi.
Finally pack the bags, firstly check, secondly book taxi.
Secondly firstly pack bags, finally check passport.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't forget your passport, would you?
You wouldn't forget your passport, do you?
You wouldn't forget your passport, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't forget your passport, will you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't forget..., would you?'
